title: Other religions
hookLine: the Vatican sends greetings for Vesak, Diwali and other feasts

cards: A letter goes out from an office in Rome, addressed to Buddhist friends, for the feast of Vesak. Another goes to Hindu friends, for Diwali, the festival of lights.

They come from the Vatican's office for interreligious dialogue, and they read like letters between neighbors: good wishes for the feast, a few lines on something both communities care about, an invitation to work together.
Behind them sits one sentence from the Second Vatican Council. Today, other religions.

teach.h: NOTHING TRUE AND HOLY IS REJECTED.
teach.b: On day three hundred twenty-one, that sentence was your line: nothing true is rejected. Here it is in full.
Nostra Aetate, a little before its paragraph on Muslims, says the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions.

teach.h: OTHER PATHS DESCRIBED IN THEIR OWN TERMS.
teach.b: First it describes other paths in their own terms.

Of Hinduism, it says people contemplate the divine mystery, express it through myth and philosophy, and seek release through ascetic practice, deep meditation, and a loving, trusting flight toward God.

Of Buddhism, it says it recognizes the insufficiency of this changing world, and teaches a way to reach perfect liberation or supreme illumination. The council isn't grading anyone. It's listening and describing.

Then a balancing line, in two halves. The Church looks with sincere respect on ways of acting and teaching that differ from its own, because they often reflect a ray of the truth that enlightens all people.
And in the same breath it proclaims Christ, who in John's Gospel says, in the Douay-Rheims, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life."

teach.h: RESPECT AND PROCLAMATION, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Respect and proclamation sit in one paragraph, not as rivals.
Finally, it urges Catholics toward dialogue and collaboration with followers of other religions, with prudence and love, recognizing and promoting the spiritual and moral goods found among them.

teach.h: I AM THE WAY, AND THE TRUTH, AND THE LIFE.
teach.b: A letter for Diwali is one small way of doing that. It doesn't say all paths are the same. It says: we see your feast, and we wish you well.

how: A Vatican office for interreligious dialogue sends messages of greeting for feasts such as Vesak and Diwali, and some Catholic dioceses and parishes join local interfaith gatherings or send greetings to neighboring communities for their feasts.

it speaks of Hindu contemplation and meditation and the Buddhist path to liberation, with respect.
the council says all religions are the same
it respects what is true and holy in them, and in the same paragraph says the Church proclaims Christ.
the Vatican's feast greetings are only for Christian holidays
its office for interreligious dialogue sends greetings for feasts like Vesak and Diwali.

games.q: a coworker is getting ready for Diwali. you're Catholic. what fits the practice the council started?
o: wish her and her family a happy Diwali.
games.why: a greeting of respect is what Rome itself does: its office for dialogue sends Diwali greetings to Hindu friends.

practice: Let a name come: someone you know who keeps a feast you don't, Diwali, Vesak, Passover, Eid, Vaisakhi, Lunar New Year, whatever is real in your own circle.
Shape a greeting for it in plain words, the name of their feast and that you wish them and their family well; nothing more is needed. If you pray, you can hold their household before God.

wordCard.voice: Other religions. Nostra Aetate says the Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in them, and asks Catholics for dialogue with prudence and love. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: in our time, the opening words and the name of the council's declaration on other religions.

carryVoice: Your line: greetings of respect. A feast noticed, and a neighbor wished well. Go gently.
